We have a camera, which we can select by clicking on it, left clicking on it. We have a cube, and we have a light, which again we can select any of these by left clicking on them. ### Manipulating Objects

Alright, in this one we're going to take a look at how to manipulate objects in Blender. So let's get right to it. First make sure your cube is selected by clicking on it, again left click on it. G key is to grab and you can see that when I move my mouse, the cube follows along with it. If I right click, it will not confirm the movement and it will just place it back to where it was. R is going to rotate our object, as you can see right there. Once again, if I right click, it will not confirm the rotation. And if I left click, it will confirm it. If you hit R twice, so if I hit R once and then a second time, you can see we could tumble rotate it. So if you hit R just once, it will rotate it from whatever view that you're in. And hitting it a second time will allow for you to tumble rotate it. Once again, left clicking to confirm and right clicking to not confirm. And then we have the S key. S key is to scale it. Once again, right click to not confirm and left click to confirm, as you can see right there. Pretty awesome. So once again, G to grab, R to rotate, S to scale. ### Keyframe & Animation

All right. And this one we're going to go ahead and go over animation because we do use some animation throughout this course. So I want to go over keyframes and how to use them and what they are. Shift right arrow to go to the end frame, which is frame 250. So right here I'm going to go to frame one. Next let's take a look at keyframes and what they are because these are what allow for us to do animations. So right here you can see that my timeline header is on frame one right here. If I select an object and hover my mouse over the 3D viewport. I could hit the I key, and you can see that it basically adds what's called a keyframe, which is this little orange or yellow diamond right here. You could also see that the transform properties right here or the transform channels are now yellow. Same with right here. If I hit the end key you can see that they are now yellow. This indicates that there is a keyframe with these values on this frame right here. Now what is a keyframe? Basically, a keyframe is telling blender that hey, on this frame, frame one, this cube or this object is going to have a location of this. In this case, zero. A rotation of this which is zero, and a scale of one. So here on this frame it has these values. If we then move ahead to say frame ten I could then hit the g key, move the cube and move it away. And then right here, I could go ahead and hit the I key once again. Now, before I do that, you can see that the location channels are a slightly different color. They're more of an orange color. And that's because from frame one right here to then frame ten where we've moved this, you can see that this color is indicating that there's a change in the location from frame 1 to 10. And if I hit the I key once again with my mouse hovered over here, you can see it turns to this yellow color, meaning that there is now a key frame with these values on frame ten. So now on frame one we have it at these values location zero. And on frame ten we have it at this location of 0.4, 2.1 and 1.7. So these key frames are what allow for objects to be animated in blender. Pretty cool. Now of course these key frames we could also do keyframes for rotation. So if I go over here and if I go to frame ten, you can see once again we have keyed the rotation and scale. So the rotation here is at zero. If I go to frame 20 hit the R key. So now you can see that the rotation is being animated as well. Pretty awesome. Now by default with the Ikea, it's just going to go ahead and insert a keyframe for all the channels. And this is based on the preferences. So if I go to Edit Preferences over here under animation you can see we have keyframes. ### Rigidy Body Types & Mass

All right. It is time for some rigid body madness in blender. So this first section is all about rigid bodies. Now what are rigid bodies in blender? Well, here if we select our cube go to the physics tab which is this little icon. You can see that right here we have rigid body. So let's select that. Now a rigid body in blender is like a solid object that doesn't change shape when it moves or bumps into things. Think of it like a wooden block or a metal ball or something that's solid, where no matter how much we push it, pull it, drop it or collide it, it stays the same shape. And that's what rigid bodies are. This allows for us to make solid objects move in a realistic way, such as if we have a solid object falling, rolling or colliding as it would in the real world. So again, rigid body allows for us to do that without changing the shape of the object. It stays rigid as the name implies. ### Damping Translation & Rotation

All right. In this one we're going to go ahead and take a look at the dynamics. And we're going to take a look at the damping translation and the rotation. So right here let's delete everything except for one cube. So right here we have one single cube. And I'm just going to put it in the first collection. So right here we have damping translation and the damping rotation. The rotation right here is also damping. So first of all what is damping. It would be helpful to know what that is or understand what that is. So damping in blender is referring to the reduction of motion over time due to either resistance from different forces, such as friction or air resistance. So here the damping is going to be how quickly it's going to lose its motion both linearly. So the linear is the translation And angularly. Angularly is the rotation or the or the angular motion, and this helps us to create a more realistic rigid body simulation by reducing the energy of the moving object. So again, just like in real life, if you move an object, there's going to be air resistance. It's going to gradually slow down. If a ball rolls down a hill, it's going to gradually slow down from the friction which we looked at before, but also the air resistance as well. So right here we have damping translation. So this right here is going to reduce the linear velocity or the speed at which the object moves in a straight line. So here you can see if I just play this let's go ahead and delete these cubes. Let's just have one cube. If I play this it falls like so. However if I increase this to let's say 0.7, you can see that there is more air resistance and it's losing the speed at which it's moving. If I put it to one, it's not going to move at all because there is so much damping or reduction of the movement or energy. But if I put this to like 0.9, you can see that right here. There's lots of air resistance as you can see right here. So again it reduces the velocity or the speed at which it goes. So right here the higher the damping for the translation the faster the objects will slow down. And again this acts like air resistance. So right here once again if we create a kind of hill right here let's hit E to extrude that GS. Bring it down X bring it over. And we could just bring this over here. If I put the damping to zero you could see what we get here. Let's also make sure to put this to mesh for the shape. So right here if I play this you can see with a damping of zero. We have this right here. If I put the damping not to one because otherwise it won't move. But if I put it to like 0.8 or so, you can see that we have this right here where again it has a lot of air resistance as you can see right there. So that's the damping translation. Again it damps the translation or the movement. Or again it reduces the movement over time. Again damping is just reducing. So this is going to reduce the movement and the rotation. It's going to reduce or damp the rotation. So right here let's go ahead and put the damping translation I believe it was at 0.1 actually it doesn't matter because we're going to add a new object for this second one. So the second one the rotation right here. This is going to control the reduction of the angular or the rotational velocity. So basically if something is rotating such as a ball rolling down a hill it will reduce the rotation of that ball more or less, depending on if we put this lower or higher. So the higher this is, the faster it will stop spinning and the lower the slower it will stop spinning. So for example here, if we hit shift A and add in a UV sphere, and right here on this UV sphere let's add a rigid body, set it to active. Now to be able to see this actually spinning. Of course I could increase the translation as well on top of the rotation. So now it's going to have damping or slowing down of the movement and the rotation. So you could think of this. ### Rigid Body World Settings

All right. And this one we're going to go ahead and take a look at the rigid body world settings. So let's go to our scene tab right here. And once again you can see that we have this rigid body world tab right here. So this right here is going to allow for us to configure and set up the different parameters for our rigid body simulation. So let's go over the settings. The first one that we have right here is the collection. This is basically going to tell us which collection is going to contain the objects for our rigid body simulation. By default it's set to rigid body world. But we could change that if we want. For example, if I go ahead let's add a cube right here. You could go ahead and do the same thing. And we're going to make it a rigid body. So now when I play this this falls. Let me go into solid view as well. So now with this cube, I'm going to go ahead and hit the M key and move it to a new collection. And I'll just name it test one and I'll click create. So now you can see that here in the collections. Let me go ahead and collapse this collection so that we can see it. We have our dominoes in this one and our cube in test one. So here if I go to the rigid body world I can go ahead and x this one out and select the test one collection. So now it's only going to take into account the objects that are in this test one collection. So if I play it you can see that the dominoes don't play. Also it doesn't fall on the floor since this is in a different collection, as you can see right there. If I change this back to either rigid body world or collection because again, our dominoes are in this collection, you can see that when I play it, the dominoes play. It interacts with the floor, but this one is no longer active or a part of the rigid body simulation. And there we go. Now, if I go back to this rigid body world collection right here, this is just going to include everything. So as you can see, this includes this one that's in this collection. And the dominoes that are in the collection collection. So the rigid body world will include all of them. Pretty cool. So I'm just going to leave it to rigid body world for now. All right then right here we have constraints. This is going to be the collection for our constraints. So again this is going to define the constraints that are used in our rigid body simulation. We haven't taken a look at constraints yet. We will in a future video. But you can see here on the cube if I go to the physics tab right here, let me collapse this up. You can see that we have rigid body constraint right here. And if I go back here and on this constraints for the rigid body constraints, I select for example, this test one collection. You can see it's going to go ahead and add a rigid body constraint. And then we're able to have this in that simulation. And in that collection again we'll take a look at this in a different video. So let's go ahead and hit control Z to remove that rigid body constraint. And this one as well makes sure that that's removed. Then the next one is really cool. This is the speed of the simulation. By default the value of one is going to be real world speed or real world time. So the simulation is going to run in real time, as you can see right there. But we could go ahead and increase this, which will make our simulation run faster, as you can see right there. Or if we want to run it in slow motion, we could decrease this, for example, to 0.18 or so. And now you can see it's going to be in slow motion and we have these dominoes falling slowly. Very cool. So again, speed of one is the default speed. If you put it to less it will run slower or in slow motion. You put it higher. It will run faster. Then right here we have split impulse for this. Let's go to our cube right here and let's hit shift d, z and duplicate two more cubes on top of each other. So first of all, let's take a look at what impulse is so right here. Impulse in rigid body and in blender is going to be the sudden change in the momentum of our objects that occurs during a collision. So right here when we play this you can see that there's a certain change in momentum of the objects when they collide. Same thing with our dominoes over here. So the impulses are going to be responsible for the immediate effect of the collision, such as if an object bounces off of another object. So again, the impulse is going to be the force that's applied during a collision, and this is going to cause a change in the velocity. This can make the objects bounce, slide or just stop as they do right here. So these ones are just stopping. These ones right here are kind of bouncing as they hit the floor, but not really. They're kind of stopping as well. But that is the impulse. So right here this split impulse is going to improve the stability of when things collide with each other. Because normally when these objects collide with each other, it can cause a large change in the velocity. And this leads or it can lead to jittering or instability in the simulation. So this right here is going to go ahead and help with that. This is going to help to reduce the instability of the collision by splitting the collision responses in two separate calculations. So instead of calculating all the collisions together, it splits them and it's able to calculate them separately and again help with the jittering or the issues that can occur when things are colliding. So here with the split impulses it's going to split first the collision of these rigid bodies. So it's going to split the primary collision of these which is going to change the velocity. And then it's going to go ahead and calculate the separation of the objects and make sure that they don't penetrate or intersect with each other. So it's separating out those two calculations. And again this will help to reduce jittering and increase the stability of the simulation. So this can be very useful especially if objects are stacking. Now this is a pretty simple simulation. So even if we enable this you can see that not much is happening, but if you have issue in your simulation where you have a bunch of stacked objects and you're seeing that there's a lot of jittering and it's not calculating it properly, you could enable this split impulse right here, and it will basically calculate it in different steps so that it has a smoother result. In this case, this is pretty simple, but I'm sure as we go through this course, we'll probably use this option on more complex simulations. Then we have substeps per frame. Now again, these names might sound complicated, but the Substeps per frame is going to be how many calculations blender is going to do per frame for our simulation to keep it accurate. So the more substeps, the more precision. But obviously it's going to take more time to compute, and the less substeps the less precision, but it will be faster. So again, this is how many calculations per frame it's going to take to make it more realistic. So you can see by default it's set to ten. So every frame it's taking ten calculations for the rigid body. And you can see it works fine. But if I put this all the way to one, you can see that the dominoes and the cubes are not going to calculate properly because there's only one calculation per frame. So here these are just acting weird. And then the dominoes are kind of falling through the floor and they're not interacting properly as you can see, because there's only one calculation per frame for how the rigid body should interact and act. You could kind of think of this as taking more snapshots for an event to capture more of that moment. So in this case, we are capturing more of how the rigid body should act and interact with other rigid bodies. If I put this to, let's say, 100 or 500, in this case, you can see that there's not really a difference. In fact, it's acting even worse with that domino. But you can see it's much slower. As you can see my frames per seconds, but there's not much difference between 500 or 468 and ten. So right here at a default of ten it seems to work good. If you notice that there's some issues with it calculating once again you could increase this, but I wouldn't increase it too much. Probably around 20 to 30. But usually at the default ten it should work just fine. So I'm just going to leave it to ten here for now. Then we have solver iterations right here. This is going to be the number of times that it's going to try to solve the calculations for each step. So the more iterations that we have, the more accurate and stable the simulation will be. But once again it's going to take more computation. You can think of this like checking your homework multiple times to make sure that it's correct. So again, this one is like taking multiple snapshots to capture every single moment that's happening in the simulation. And this one is like double checking those moments or those snapshots. So here you can see that you can't drag this any lower. However we could just type in a lower number such as one. And you can see what that gives us. Now there's not much difference here. And if I increase this. And that's also because this is set to ten. If I set this to three and play this with three and one, you can see that we get this right here. If I put this to let's say 89, you can see that we get this right here. So again both of these values are going to help to basically calculate the simulation better. By default. These are both set to ten. So I'm going to set these to ten. Once again I would just leave these to the default unless you notice you have issues. So if you have issues with it jittering or not interacting properly, you could split the impulses right here. And or you could change these values and increase them. ### Rigid Body Constraint Crashes & Fixes

All right. This is just a quick little video to show you some crashing issues that can happen when using rigid body constraints. So right here if I go and again we're going to be using rigid body constraints. But I want to show you this before so that you're not surprised if it crashes while you're doing this. So right here if we go to the physics tab and I add a rigid body, if I hit shift D, duplicate it, select both of these. I'm just going to go to Object Rigid Body and connect to add a rigid body constraint. Now right here it's basically these two rigid bodies are connected by this rigid body constraint. Now one of the crashing issues that can happen is if we delete one of the two rigid body objects while the animation is playing. So you can see here if I play this and delete one of these cubes, it's going to crash sometimes. So let me play this. Delete the cube. Let me hit control Z. Undo it. Delete the cube again. Gan control Z, undo it again, delete it and you can see that it's crashed. Let me go ahead and reopen blender and let me reset this up right here. So the reason it's doing that let me go to rigid Bodies Connect. The reason it's doing that is because right here we're deleting one of the cubes that's connected to this rigid body constraint. And this rigid body constraint is controlling both of the cubes. But since one of the cubes no longer exists, it's freed from the memory. Blender is going to crash because it's trying to access the data of a deleted object. So it just crashes. So right here the constraint is still holding a pointer or a memory reference to the deleted object. And when it's trying to access this data or this memory for this deleted object, it causes an error because the memory points to something that no longer exists or that no longer belongs to the deleted object. So we have blender crashing. So the solution is to automatically remove any constraints that are connected to a rigid body. When that rigid body is deleted. So this will help to prevent blender from trying to constrain something that no longer exists. So obviously if we delete this cube right here, we no longer need this constraint. And we should delete it because otherwise it's going to try to access the data of this deleted object. So we want to delete this. Otherwise it could cause it to crash. Now another issue with the crashing. Let me just start a blank slate and rigid body and let me go to rigid body and connect. Now another issue that can happen when it crashes is when you're undoing after an animation. So right here, for example, if I play this and then here if I go ahead and move this cube like so, and then play it again and then hit control Z to undo that and play it, you can see it crashes. So here let me reopen blender. And so you can see that here. It just crashes when I'm just undoing it. Now the reason this happens is because when we play the animation, it's caching and storing data with the animation here. But if we move the cube and then play it again, it's storing new information. However, when we hit control Z it's going to revert it back to this. However, hitting control Z or undoing it doesn't necessarily reset all of the internal data correctly, especially when we're using rigid bodies and constraints. This works fine with rigid bodies, but when the constraints come in, it kind of acts a little bit wonky. So here it might still have some leftover information from the animation before even after undoing it. So here it might still have information about the old position of the cube and the constraint that was created during the animation before. And so now when we play it, if it still has that old information, it's going to attempt to use the outdated or invalid information, and obviously if it no longer exists, it's going to crash. Now here you can see that it's working this time because it actually undid all the previous information. But sometimes when you do this and hit control Z, if it doesn't remove all the previous information, it will crash. Because again, it's trying to read data that is no longer there. As you can see right here, it's working fine. But then out of the blue, out of nowhere, you'll hit control Z and it will just crash. So keep these two in mind when you delete an object or a constraint. Or if you hit control Z and undo it could cause some crashing issues. So what I recommend once again, if you delete one of these objects and you delete it, for example, right here, delete it. Make sure to delete the constraint that's associated with it because obviously you no longer need it. And if you move an object. If you don't need to hit Ctrl Z. As you can see right there, it crashed. If you don't need to hit Ctrl Z, let me go back here. Shift D, duplicate it and let me put rigid body and connect. Connect. Rigid body. Connect. If you don't need to undo it for example let's say you play it and then you move the cube over here instead of undoing it. Just grab the cube and place it back in the position that you want. Unless it's a specific position. And also make sure to save often because again, as you can see, sometimes when you undo it, it's going to crash, sometimes it doesn't. But then just out of the blue it will just crash. So if you don't necessarily need to put it back in the exact position, just hit the G key and grab it instead of hitting undo. And that will not cause that crashing issue. All right. Hope this helps you out. Just keep those things in mind when you're using rigid body constraints. I'll see you in the next one. Ciao for now.

### Creating Car Drivers

All right. In this one we're going to go ahead and add the drivers for our back wheels and front wheels. No I don't mean a driver like a person in the car, but in blender a driver is a value or something that influences or drives another value or another object. So in this case here, if we wanted to change the speed of these wheels, the back wheels which moves the car, we would have to go into each of these motor empties and change the value, which is really annoying. So we're just going to have a single object that drives this value on the two back wheels to move the speed, and a driver that moves the rotation of the car for this motor constraint right here. This one right here, right there. That way we don't have to go in here and change these values. But we could just do it by moving an object. Now right here. Let's do the back wheels first. Or the speed of the car here on the motor constraint, if we put the target velocity to zero on both of these. So let's put it to zero. The target velocity if we play it. So right here they should not rotate or move. And this is what we want. Sometimes it will get stuck and still have the same values or cash that you had before. So just go ahead and uncheck angular and check it back and it should update it. So now what we're going to do is we're going to change our outliner to the 3D viewport right here. ## Cloth Physics

### Cloth Quality Stiffness & More

All right. We are now moving on to the cloth physics in blender. We've done the rigid bodies. Now it's time for cloth. Now the cloth. Physics in blender, obviously, as the name implies, allows for us to create realistic cloth simulations. Now this could be great for things such as clothing, flags, curtains, or really anything that we need to act like a cloth. So over here, let's go ahead. Let's delete this cube and shift a, let's add in a plane and let's go to the physics tab. And right here we're going to go ahead and enable the cloth physics. All right let's take a look at all these different options right here. You can see if I play this we get this right here which is very very boring. The cloth is just falling. So let's go ahead and hit shift A let's add a UV sphere and bring it below the cloth. Now how do we get the cloth to collide with this? It is not a rigid body passive that we want to add as that will only interact with rigid bodies, but instead it is a collision. So collision allows for things like cloth to collide with it. So here let's go ahead and add a collision to this sphere. We'll take a look at the settings a little bit later. All right let's go back to our cloth. And now when we play it you can see the cloth falls on top of the sphere. Let's also right click the sphere and shade it smooth. Very very boring. Not really cloth like this is a very stiff cloth. The reason that it's acting this stiff is because right here, if we go into edit mode of our cloth, you can see we only have four vertices. So yes, it is very important how many vertices you have for your cloth simulations whereas rigid bodies, the rigid bodies wouldn't change or deform. Obviously cloth is going to change and deform, and for it to change and deform, it needs more geometry. So right here I'm just going to right click subdivide. And in the bottom left here I'm going to increase the number of cuts to ten. And let me go ahead and close this tool shelf with the T key. So now if I play it you can see we get this right here. Pretty cool. Let's also right click shade it smooth. So now we have this right there. All right. We have a very basic cloth setup. Let's take a look at these different options. The first one is the quality steps. This is going to determine the overall quality of our cloth simulation. The higher the value the more quality and the more accurate it will be. But obviously it's going to take more computation. So right here for example, if I put this to one, this is going to be a low quality computation and it's going to be less accurate. As you can see right there. This interacts like so if I put this to let's say 80, you can see that we get this right here. Now right now it's not really doing much of a difference between 1 and 80. So right here instead of the UV sphere let's actually hit shift A add a monkey or Suzanne and right click shade smooth make Suzanne a collision. And now let's go ahead and play this cloth simulation. So here you can see what's happening. The cloth acts like. So if I put this to one you can see that right here. The cloth is not really sliding off as much. And it's kind of staying stuck up here because again the quality of the simulation is less. If I put this to 80, you can see it's much higher. Now obviously you wouldn't crank it to a value of 80. You'll probably put it in between a value of five and maybe 30. Again, it all depends on what you're doing. But again this is going to be the quality, the overall quality of the simulation. So again if you notice that things are not simulating properly and the cloth is not falling or interacting as it should, it might be the quality steps that are not high enough, as you can see right there. All right. Let's set this to the default of five. Again we'll look at all these options even more as we use them. The quality step can also help with reducing jittering or the cloth passing through itself as well. So again it increases or decreases the overall quality. Then we have the speed multiplier right here. This is going to adjust the speed of the cloth simulation without changing any of the physics settings. So you can see right here if I play this it has this certain speed. If I increase this to ten, for example, it's going to multiply the speed of it, as you can see right there. Now you can see that a speed of ten right here we have a lot of jittering. And again this has to do with the quality. So here if I increase the quality to say 33 and play it, you can see that there's a lot less jittering. All right let me go ahead and put the quality back to five. So again the speed multiplier just multiplies the speed that it goes at without changing any of the other settings. Let me put this back to one. So again the higher this is the faster it will play. If we bring it down it will play like it's playing in slow motion, as you can see right there. So we could put it to a lower or higher value. Pretty cool. All right. Let's set this back to one and this back to five. Then we have vertex mass right here. This is going to be the mass of each of the vertices of our cloth mesh. Now the heavier the cloth or the vertex mass, the heavier it will be, and the less it will be affected by things such as wind or forces. So here you can see that it's set to 0.3. If I play it, we have this right here. If I set this, for example, to 11 and play it, you can see that it doesn't really do any difference. And again, that's because this has to do with forces or when the cloths collide with each other. So for example right here back to point three I'm just going to hit shift A and go to force field and add a force. Again we're going to take a look at force fields later. But for now let me just add one down here and right here. If I play this with a mass or a vertex mass of 0.3, you can see that right here on the force field. Let me put the strength to ten. And when I play this Let me also bring it up a little bit like so. And let me put the strength maybe higher to 500. There we go. So you can see here with the strength of 500, you can see that this is raising up. And the vertices or the mass of this cloth is 0.3. But if I change this to let's say ten right here and play it, you can see that it's much heavier. Again, this is kind of like the mass on the rigid body physics. ## Particle Systems

### Emission Particle System

All right. It is time for a new section, which means in this one we're going to take a look at the particle system. Now the particle system is really cool. What it allows for us to do is simulate and create various effects that involve a large amount of particles or objects. This could allow for us to create things such as rain or dust or hair, fur, grass, or distribute objects all over our scene, etc. they are really awesome. They also interact with force fields and things like collisions etc. and they are just really cool. So let's go ahead and take a look at these over here. If we go to the physics tab, you can see that we don't have particles here because the particles have their own tab right here. Right here you can see we have a plus icon to add a new particle system and a minus icon to remove it. We also have a little drop down right here with various options, as you can see right here, mainly to be able to copy the particle system or duplicate it. Now over here we have what is called the particle system index. So this is going to be kind of containers for the particle systems. Right here we have the particle system itself. So here for example if we rename the particle system to test one you can see that this particle system container or index has this particle system in it. We can add however many particle system containers as we want. So for example if I click the plus icon you can see I have another particle system. On this particle system container. I could click the drop down and select my test one particle system. So now this particle system and this one both have the same particle system on them. Now these particle systems are applied in order. So it applies the first one first then the second one, then it would apply the third, fourth, etc. so again, these containers, you could basically have any kind of particle system on it, whether it's the same one or a different one as you can see right there. So right here let's go ahead and hit the minus icon to remove one. And let's just have one for now. So this particle system container or index has the particle system test one right here. So here we could rename it. We could also rename this as well if we want. So I could rename this to test one right here as well. Now over here we have two little different options right here. This will create a new particle system. So if I click on this you can see we have test 1001. Let's name this to test two. And then right here if we click in the little drop down here you can see we have all our particle systems. Right here we have test two selected which you can see right there. But we have all these other ones from what we did previously, such as test one. Now you can see that on all of these they have a little zero on them. The zero means that these have zero users, or that these particle systems are not assigned anywhere. They're just there, but they're not assigned anywhere. You can see if I select test one here. Now test two has a zero next to it because again it has zero users. Now let's say we have test one here. And let's say on test two we change the settings. And we still want to have test two. The issue right here is if I go to test one you can see that here I have all of these. But if I go ahead and save my file file save as. So here I've saved it. If I reopen it because these have zero users they're going to disappear. So here if I reopen it you can see that here. After reopening it I have none of these particle systems that had zero users. So if I want to save those particle systems, even though they're not being used, for example, here, if I create a new one, name it test two right here, I can make this a fake user. You can see we have this little shield fake user. So this is going to save the block. As it says it's going to save the data even if it has no users. So if I click this on test two and then I change to test one. You can see that here. Test one is being used. So we're good. But test two is not being used. However now instead of having a zero it has an F for a fake user, meaning that it will still be saved even though it's not being used. So here, if I save this again, save and I reopen it, it will still be there with a fake user right there. So we will still have it now. Right now the file keeps getting corrupted and not opening properly. I think it's because I'm on 4.3 alpha and there's a bug, but that's what the fake user will do. It will save it so that you could still have it even though it's not being used. All right then right here we have emission and hair. So first we're going to take a look at emission. As you can see with the emitter as the name implies it's going to emit or shoot out particles with hair. As the name implies it's going to give us hair strands like so. And with this we could do much more as well. Same with the emitter. But for now, let's take a look at the emitter. So here first section we have is emission. Now this has to do with the particles emitting. We have the number right here. Pretty self-explanatory. This is going to be the number or how many particles we have. You can see right now we have 1000 particles. If I set this to three we will have three particles. Three is the loneliest number. I think it's two, but still right here. This seems pretty lonely for sure. So that's the number right there. Changes the number of particles. I'm going to put it back to 1000. Then we have seed right here. The seed is going to randomize the particle emission. So if we change the seed it will randomize how they emit and from where they emit. So it will give you a different pattern of these particles. So for example right here if I play it you can see that we have this right here. In fact if I just go forward with my right arrow you can see that on frame two the particles are here. If I change the seed you can see that it changes where they are. So this will change or randomize from where the particles emit so that you could have a different distribution of them or a different pattern. These are already pretty random. So usually you don't really need to change this unless you have a particle system that's exactly the same, then you would change the seed on the other particle system so that they don't emit from the same exact spot. So once again that is the seed. Keep in mind that all these values are animatable as well. Then we have the frame start and end. Pretty self-explanatory. This is the frame where the particle system starts. So right now it's starting on frame one and it's going to end on frame 200. As you can see right here, if we let it go all the way to 200 which is right here, the particles will stop emitting, as you can see right there. I could change the frame, start to say 50 right here and now. The particles will only start emitting at frame 50. Or I could put the end of this to frame 60. And now they will only emit from frame 50 to 60. As you can see right there. Pretty cool. All right I'm going to set this back to one and 200. Then we have the lifetime of the particles right here. So this is going to be the lifetime or how long the particles last after they've been emitted. And this is in frames. So right now you can see that the particles last for 50 frames and then they disappear as you can see right here. So from when they emit they're alive or they last for 50 frames and then they disappear. But we could change this lifetime. So if we put it to ten, as you can see right here, they will last for ten frames and then disappear. If we put the lifetime to, let's say 200, you can see that right here. They're going to last for 200 frames and then disappear only after 200 frames. As you can see right there, they're still going and now they're starting to disappear. Pretty cool. All right. Let's put the lifetime back to 50 as well. Then we have the lifetime randomness right here. Or the lifetime random. So this, as the name implies, will change the randomization for the lifetime of the particles. Right now, all the particles have a lifetime of 50. So after 50 frames, they disappear. But right here, as we start to increase this, it's going to increase the randomness for the lifetime of the particles. So some of them will disappear faster and some will disappear slower. As you can see if I increase this quite a lot. So right here these particles have more lifetime. And then we have some that are disappearing here that have a shorter lifetime. This can be useful. For example, let's say we're making fireworks and we have some particles fade out faster than others. Instead of having all the particles fade out at the same time or the same spot like so. Another thing to keep in mind with the frame start and end, and the number right here, the number of particles will be emitted within this time frame. So if we have the frame start at one and the end to 200, it's going to emit the thousand particles within that time frame between 1 and 200. But if we have the frame start at one and the end to one as well, you can see that all of them are going to be emitted all at once, as you can see right there. If we have the end frame to ten, that means that all 1000 particles are going to be emitted within those frames between frame one and frame ten, as you can see right there. So again, the number of particles will be emitted in the time span of the start and end frame. The more distance you put between these, the longer it will take to emit all of the particles. For example, once again if we put four particles. So right here we have the four particles emitting within that time span. But once again if I put this frame start to one and end frame to one, you can see that the four particles are emitted on that single frame. So with that that is the settings. ### Particle System Source

All right. So let's go ahead and take a look at these next settings here. I put these settings. Let me put this to 1000 again. So I have the default settings 1000 start frame one and frame 200 lifetime 50. The next option is the source right here. So the source is basically going to be the source from where these emit. The first drop down that we have is emit from. So we have faces right here. You can see that here with it set to faces. Let me go into wireframe as it's going to be easier to see. You can see that it's emitting from the faces. As you can see pretty self-explanatory. It's going to emit it from the surface of the faces if we change this to vertices, as you can see here, it's going to emit it from the vertices of the mesh. If we change it to volume right here, it's going to emit from inside the cube. You can see this especially if in edit mode I scale this up. You can see the difference with faces right here, where it's emitting from the faces and volume right here where it's emitting also from the inside of the cube, as you can see right there. Very cool. So that's the first option emit from. Let's go ahead and just leave it to faces. Then we have use modifier stack. This is going to make it so that it takes into account any modifiers that are applied to our emission object such as subdivision surface modifier. So you can see that here. If I go to the modifiers once again the particle system is a modifier. But here if I hit control to add a subsurface level of two. And here again this is very important what order these are in. So we want to put the subdivision surface modifier before the particle system. And then right here we also want to make sure that the levels viewport and render is the same as it says right here. When you hover over it, you can see that you want to make sure that they are the same as it will give you correct results, whereas if it's not, it may not work properly. Now right here you can see that if I enable this or disable this, we see a little bit of a difference, but we see it even more if we change this from faces to vertices. So with it disabled, you can see that it's not taking into account the subdivision surface modifier where right here it's just emitting from the eight vertex points as if there's no subdivision surface modifier. But if I enable use modifier stack, it will take all the new vertices that are applied from the subdivision surface modifier. And you can see that we have particles emitting from all of those. So again if I go to the modifiers and turn off optimal display, you can see that we have all of these vertices now on the mesh. Whereas if I turn on optimal display or if we didn't have this, we only have these four vertices. So again this use modifier stack is going to use the modifiers in the emission of the particle system, not just the base mesh. So again if we enable this the particles will be influenced by changes made by the modifiers. All right let's go ahead and remove this modifier. And I'm going to go back to particles. Change this back to faces. And I'm going to disable use modifier stack. Then right here we have the distribution. The distribution is going to be how the particles are distributed across the emitter objects. Right here you can see it's set to Jittered by default. Now with it set to jitter. The particles are evenly distributed across our particle system or object, with a slight randomness or jitter to avoid it being a perfectly even grid. So right here you can see they're kind of jittered. As you can see right there. We could change this to random right here with random, the particles are going to be distributed randomly across the emitter object. As you can see right there. Again with Jittered, it's more even and just has a little bit of jittering, but with random again, these are completely random. And then we have grid right here the particles are going to be distributed completely evenly like a grid, as you can see right there. So there is no randomness as you can see. Very cool. All right. And then we have some options over here depending on the distribution method. So let's take a look at these one at a time. Let's go to Jittered. So first we have random order right here. If this is enabled or checked which it is by default the particles are going to emit in a random order rather than in the exact order of the vertices, edges or faces. So you can see here the difference. If I uncheck this, you can see we get this right here where it's first emitting from the top face, then it's emitting from the side face, then it's emitting from that one, this one, this one, and then this one. If you're familiar with geometry nodes and indices or the index of the faces, again, each of these faces have an index from 0 to 5. Because right here we have six faces again zero being one of them. And it will basically emit it in that order. So it's emitting from this face, then that face, then that one, then that one. Same thing is true. If we change this to vertices, you can see we have random order by default it's enabled and it's just going to randomly distribute the particles on any of these vertices. But if we uncheck random order right here, it will do one vertex at a time. As you can see right there, it's going through one at a time based on their index. All right. ### Particles Hair Dynamics

All right. Now let's go ahead and take a look at the particle system hair dynamics. So here going back to the hair let's go ahead and enable hair dynamics. We could enable this to enable the hair dynamics. So here first we have quality steps. Now the quality steps is going to go ahead and determine the number of calculation or steps that blender is going to use to simulate the hair dynamics per frame. So again it's just like the quality steps in the rigid body or in the cloth. So the more steps we have, the higher quality and the more accurate the simulation is going to be. But it's also going to increase the computation time. So we could increase this. For example, if we have hair passing through objects or jittery movements or other things that are not accurate. So here for example with quality steps of five, we have this right here. Now keep in mind this is a very simple hair setup. And if we increase this to let's say 16, you can see that we have this right here. Again this is a very simple setup. We don't have any issues. You want to keep this at the lowest value possible where it still has good quality and it's still calculating the simulation properly. So you can see here. A value of five and a value of 26. There is no difference in how it looks but it's a lot. Slower. So you want to keep that in mind. You can see if I put it to one. We have this right here. Again almost the same as equality steps of five. Pretty much the same actually. We'll see the quality. Steps. Once we do some more complex hair simulations then we have pin goal strength right here. ### Particles Children Interpolated

All right. In this one we're going to go ahead and take a look at the interpolated children right here. Now first of all, what does interpolated mean. Because if we understand what this means we will understand what it does better. So to interpolate means that it's going to estimate or give us or insert values between two known values. So for example, if right here we have a hair strand right here and let's say we have one right here, kind of like we have right here and right here to interpolate. If we do it on simple it's just going to add children particles like so and like so. But if we do it with interpolated it's going to add values between these two values or between these two hair strands. So here it's going to interpolate and add hair strands in between them just like so. So here you can see if I turn on interpolated we have exactly that. Where we have values inserted or hair strands inserted between these major hair strands. So whereas with simple right here, it's going to generate the children exactly where the parent hairs are at the same location. And everything interpolated is going to add children hair particles in between the parent hair particles. So this is going to give us a smoother, more evenly distributed result. So if you're going to create fur or hair, you're definitely going to want to use interpolated for the most part, as simple just looks kind of bad. So you can see what that gives us on our particles over here you can see what this gives us. Again, it adds it in between. Whereas with simple everything is clumped together with interpolated. You can see everything is separated out a little bit more. Now you can see that here. These settings are exactly the same as you can see right there. We actually have two less settings right here. And we have one additional setting here, and the only difference is that we have a parting tab right here. So let's take a look at this. Once again we have the display and render amount the length the threshold the seed as you can see right here. And then the only difference right here is we have this virtual parents and long hair. So first here we have virtual parents. So with virtual parents it's going to go ahead. And it's going to make some of the children particles become virtual parents. So basically they will become parent particles. And they will help to influence the nearby particles. So you can see here at zero we have this. And as I increase this you can see how it changes the distribution of the interpolated children particles. So again with these virtual parents it's going to make some of these children particles become temporary parents. And this is going to help to control more of the distribution. Because these child particles that are now temporary parents will help to interpolate or distribute the particles much better then we have long hair right here, which we could enable or disable with the long hair. It's going to go ahead and adjust the behavior of the child particles to better suit long hair strands. So this is basically going to make it so that these children particles behave more naturally for long hair strands. So you would enable this if you have longer hair strands. And those are the only two additional options here. And then the additional tab that we have is the parting tab right here. First we have the parting tab right here. This is going to control how much hairs or strands it interpolates between the parent particles. So you can see at zero right here we have a lot of strands interpolated between these. But as I bring this up you can see at one it just looks like simple where we have nothing interpolated as I bring it down. You can see what this gives us. Pretty cool. Then right here we have a minimum and maximum. So if I put the parting up a little bit, This minimum and maximum is going to determine the maximum or minimum angles in which the parting right here will take effect. And this is relative to the direction of the parent particles. So you can see here as I increase the minimum right here. If I increase it high enough, you can see that the parting will no longer take effect, as you can see right here. So if I put it above a minimum of 90 right here, you can see that this parting no longer takes effect. So you can see that this is a 90 degree angle. Again you can see right here we have a 90 degree angle. So if I bring this above 90 the parting no longer takes effect. Let me bring this to zero. If I bring the maximum up like so, you can see that as I bring it past 90. So once it reaches past 90, which is the angle that we have here of the parent particles, you can see that it's changing how the parting is taking effect. So right here below 90 we have the parting taking effect. As I bring it above 90, you can see that it's not taking effect as much as you can see right there. So again, this is the minimum and maximum angles for the parting to take effect. Pretty cool. All right. And that is pretty much it. That is the interpolated type. And again of course we have these options over here. You can see that here. These don't do anything as you can see. Because again this is more for hair particles. It's going to ignore the curve diameter. If we change it to strip right here it's going to go ahead and render the curves as flat ribbons with rounded normals. And these ones are going to be more detailed than strands, and they're going to be able to have a diameter or thickness. So you can see here if we change it to strip and go back to the particle settings, if I change the strand shape right here, it is now doing something. So let's take a look at these options right here. So right here the strand shape is going to go ahead and control how the hair's thickness transitions from the root of the hair to the tip. So you can see here as I change this we have it tapering off or transitioning from the root to the tip. So you can see what this gives us right here. If we bring this to a lower value, you can see that it transitions off later in the hair. And as I bring this off you can see it's transitioning or tapering off earlier on the hair strand. So that's the strand shape right here. Let me put this to zero. Then we have the diameter root right here. Obviously this is the diameter for the root or the start of the hair. So if I change this you can see that this will increase the thickness of the start of the hair, as you can see right there. So you can see here this is changing the diameter of the root of the hair. Then we have the tip right here. This is the diameter for the tip of the hair or the thickness at the tip of the hair, as you can see right there. Let me put that to one as well. Then we have diameter scale right here. This is going to go ahead and multiply both the root and the tip diameters. So we could scale the entire thickness of the hair strand. So right here you can see that this multiplies both of those values. Obviously if we have the tip at zero this is going to multiply this times zero. So you can see it's not doing anything to the tip. If we put the root to zero obviously we have no hair. But right here you can see that this will multiply both of those values. Then right here we have closed tip. This is going to force the tip of the hair the scale to zero. Regardless of the tip diameter or the multiplier of the diameter scale. You can see if I uncheck this right here. The tip or the end of the hair has a certain thickness to it. But right here if we enable closed tip, no matter what these are set to, it will still taper it off into a point and have zero thickness at the tip if we enable closed tip. Very cool. ## Soft Body

### Soft Body Object

All right. In this section we're going to go ahead and take a look at soft bodies. Now soft bodies in blender are used to simulate soft or flexible objects that are going to deform when they interact with other objects or forces. Now they were primarily designed to add secondary motion to animation, like jiggling for body parts of a moving character, but we can use them for things such as jello or anything that's soft and that deforms. So right here, let's go to the physics tab and let's select Soft Body. Let's also bring the cube up. Shift a add a mesh plane, scale it up in edit mode and make this a collision. All right. So right here if we play this you can see not much is happening. It's just kind of oscillating right here. And that's because of the goal. Let's uncheck the goal so that it falls down. And now you can see that we have this soft body kind of jiggling physics which is pretty cool. Now right here the first option we have is obviously collision collection. This just like before is going to be the collection for the collision objects. We've gone over this many times, but once again, if I go ahead and duplicate this and I put this one M key on a new collection, and I go over here, and now this one is on collection one and this one is on collection two. If I select our first collection, which has this one, it's going to go past this one and interact with that one. If I select the collection number two you can see it's going to interact with this one. Pretty cool. All right. Let me go ahead and remove the collection right there. Then we have object right here. So here under object we first have friction. Now the friction is going to control how much the surrounding medium. In this case it is just the air around the cube is going to slow down the movement of the soft body vertices. So here the higher the friction the more it's going to move slowly, kind of like it's falling through thick liquid. So you can see here at 0.5 we get this right here. But if I increase the friction you can see now it looks like it's falling through thick liquid. Or if I put it at zero we get this right here. And if I put it to 50, you can see we get this right here. So again this is going to be how much the surrounding medium in this case the air around our cube is going to slow down the movement of the soft body. I'm going to put this back to 0.5. All right then we have the mass. Obviously the mass is going to set the weight of the soft body vertices. So the higher the mass is the heavier the vertices are and the heavier vertices are going to obviously resist things such as changing or outside forces or deformation more. So it's going to make them harder to stop or move. So here you can see a mass of one. We got this right here. If I put the mass to 22, you can see that we get this right here where it compresses a lot more because it's a lot heavier. Also, you can see another thing. If I re-enable goal and play it, you can see it doesn't do much. But if I increase the mass to like three you can see we get a little bit more weight. If I put this high enough to let's say 11 or so, you can see here that the cube let me actually put it to 22. You can see here that the cube now falls because it has enough mass. Very cool. All right. Let me uncheck the goal again and put the mass back to one. Then we have control points right here. The control point is going to allow for us to use a vertex group to assign different vertices with different mass values. So here we're able to vertex paint or assign different values. So if I go into edit mode and go to the vertex groups add a new one. And with all these vertices assign a weight of one. And then go back to my physics tab and select that group. You can see here if I play it, we get this right here. But if I go over here to my vertex groups and assign all of these a weight of zero, you can see that I get this right here. Nothing's happening. But if I go ahead and select these two vertices and assign a weight of one, you can see that all of these have a weight of zero, but these two have a weight of one. And if I play it you can see we get this right here. So we're able to specify the weight of the vertices using a vertex group, and that's what the control point is. As you can see right there. Pretty cool. All right let me x that out then. Here we have simulation. Right here we have the speed. This is going to control how fast the simulation plays. So you can see here at a speed of one. We have this right here. If I change this to three you can see we have that right there. If I change this to let's say 0.01, you can see it's not even moving. So if I increase this to like 0.3, you can see that we have this right here and it's moving in slow motion. So again the speed will control the speed or how fast the simulation plays. All right I'm going to put that back to one then. Right here we have the cash. We've already taken a look at the cash many times. So I'm not going to go over this again. If you want to know what the cash does check out the rigid body physics or the cloth physics. And we go over the cash quite a bit, especially in the rigid body physics section. All right. In the next one we're going to go ahead and take a look at the goal and the rest of the settings. So I'll see you there. Ciao for now. Over.

### Soft Body Goal

All right. Let's go ahead and take a look at the goal now. So let's enable goal right here. Now what does the goal do. The goal is going to be used to influence the soft body simulation by an animation. So for example keyframes or an armature or any kind of animation that's going to animate our soft body. So for example right here let's go ahead and on frame one I'm going to hit the I key to insert a keyframe I'm going to go to frame 20 G. Bring this over. Let me actually just hit G. Bring it over here I key insert a keyframe. So now if I play this you can see that here with goal enabled, we get this right here where the animation is able to influence our soft body. However, if I uncheck this, you can see that here the animation is no longer influencing the soft body. And you can see that the keyframes that we added are no longer contributing to it. Whereas if I enable goal again, this animation is influencing the soft body. Very cool. Then right here we have vertex group. So this is going to specify some vertices or a vertex group that will follow the goal more strictly or less strictly depending on the weight. So here if we go to our vertex groups and I go into edit mode right here, once again you can see that these are set to zero. And these two right here are set to a weight of one. If I just enable this group you can see that here these two vertices that are assigned a weight of one are influenced more by the goal. If I go ahead and select all of these and assign them a weight of zero, you can see that we have this right here where none of them are influenced by the goal. Obviously a weight of one. They're all influenced by the goal. Or I could just set all of these to zero and assign just a single vertex to a weight of one. And you can see that, of course we could influence it and put the weight to something other than 0 or 1, such as 0.4. And then right here you can see it has 0.4% influence on the goal, as you can see right there. Or I could select all of these right here. Assign these to 0.4. And you can see what we got right there. As opposed to if I put it to one you could see the difference. Very cool. All right. Let me go here and remove the vertex group. Then under the goal we have some other options. We have settings right here. So you can see we have stiffness and damping. So the stiffness right here is going to be the spring stiffness for the goal. So if we have a low value right here it's going to create very weak springs which are going to be more flexible. And a high value is going to create stronger springs that are going to be stiffer. So here you can see with 0.5, if I play this you can see the springiness of it. If I put it to zero. You can see we get this right here. And if I put this higher to 0.99, you can see right here the spring is a lot stiffer. Let me put it to for example 0.1. So you can see a 0.1. The spring is not stiff. And you can see it's oscillating back and forth quite a bit. Whereas a higher number it's stiffer. And you can see that the oscillation is completely different. So again this is the stiffness of the springs for the goal or how much or how stiff it oscillates when it goes back and forth. Then we have the damping right here. So the damping is going to slow down either faster or slower. The spring effect or the jiggling effect. So here you can see a damping of zero. Right now it's not slowing down again. You can see the motion of it is just continuing. But if we put the damping up to let's say 11, you can see here it basically jiggles or goes back and forth with the spring, and then it comes to a stop. So the higher this value, the faster it will come to a stop. So here you can see at zero it just continues. If I put this to let's say 50 you can see here it bounces back and forth like twice and then comes to a stop. If I put this to let's say five you can see right here, it goes back and forth and then comes to a stop as you can see right there. Very cool. Let me put the damping back to zero. And then we have strengths right here. Let me also put the stiffness to 0.5. So right here we first have default. Now the default right here is going to be the overall strength that's going to pull the vertices toward the goal position or the animated position. And this is when no vertex group is assigned right here. So right now you can see if I put this to zero, you can see that once again we have no vertices being pulled towards the goal or the animation. And if we put this to one, you can see that all of them are being pulled towards it. If I put it to like 0.5 or so, you can see that we get this kind of oscillating motion, as you can see right there. Whereas a setting of one, it just goes there and stops. So basically defines how strongly the vertices are going to stick to the animation motion. Again, when a vertex group is not assigned, you can see that if I put the vertex group right here, this is going to affect it differently. So you can see at zero we have this right here. And at one we have this right here. So obviously with the vertex group the vertices are also dictating how much they constrain to the animation. So right here let me put this back to like a 0.7 or so. And then right here we have minimum and maximum. Let me remove the group. You can see here that if I don't have a vertex group and I put the minimum and maximum we get this right here so you can see what happens when I move these values with no vertex group. But this is more for vertex groups. So if we have our vertex group right here, the minimum and maximum is going to basically dictate the minimum and maximum influence for the goal. So the minimum is going to apply to the vertices with the lowest weight. So again if we go over here let me select all these and remove them. Let me select this face right here. And on these I'm going to select or assign a low weight assign. And on these I'm going to assign a high weight. So right here the minimum is going to refer to the vertices with the lowest weight. And the maximum is going to refer to the vertices with the highest weight. So here we could control how much these vertices that have the lowest weights assigned to them, or the highest weights assigned to them Conform to the goal or the animation. So right here if I play this, you can see I have this right here. And you can see that here. These vertices with the low weight are not conforming as much to the animation. They're kind of lagging behind as you can see and falling. But if I put the minimum up to one, you can see that they follow along. Or if I put the minimum to 0.4 or 5, you can see that they follow along more. So here you can see if I put the minimum to around 0.2 and the max to one, we have this right here where the vertices assign the higher weights go all the way here, as you can see. But if I put the maximum to zero you can see that now we have this right here where those vertices are not conforming to the goal or the animation. As you can see right there. You can see here if we put the minimum to one and the max to zero, we still get it pushed like that. Because keep in mind that if the vertices have a weight of zero, that is still the lowest. So basically all these vertices right here have a low weight and they're pushing everything that way. If I were to go into edit mode and subdivide this a little bit like so and go to the vertex groups, I'm going to select everything and click remove. Then I'm going to in vertex select mode. And in wireframe assign these ones to a high weight. And I'm going to assign these ones right here to a low weight. So right here I'll assign these to a weight of zero which they already are. And then I'll assign these ones in between a slightly higher weight right here assign and these ones right here a slightly lower weight. You can see what's going to happen right here. So if I play it you can see that right now the minimum is all the way up. So it's just pushing everything. But if I put this slightly down you can see what's happening right here. So here the vertices with the lowest weight are being influenced by the animation more. As you can see right there as they are jiggling. And they have the soft body simulation to them, whereas the one with the highest weight don't have any of the soft body affecting it. If I put the max up a little bit, you can see that now this area jiggles and has soft body as well. If I put it to zero you can see we have that. So there we go. That is the goal again to break it down. The goal is basically allowing for the animation to affect the soft body. And then right here these are going to basically dictate how the soft body interacts with the goal or the animation, such as how stiff the springs should be, the damping of the animation, and the strength of how the animation and the goal interact with one another. So there we go. That is the goal setting right here. I'll see you in the next one. Ciao for now. Over.

### Soft Body Edges

All right. And this one we're going to go ahead and take a look at the soft body edges. So right here let's add a soft body and go to the edges right here. Let's also bring it up a little bit. And once again add a plane collision on the soft body. Let's disable goal so that it falls. And on the cube let's also right click subdivide it and right click subdivide it one more time. All right. So let's take a look at these edges right here. So this edges menu is going to allow for the edges of our mesh to act like springs. Now once again we've already gone over springs in the cloth section. But basically we have these invisible springs that are connected from edge to edge or vertex to vertex. And these springs create this compression and stretching motion as you can see right here as it compresses and stretches. ### Soft Body Self Collision

All right. In this one we're going to go ahead and take a look at the self-collision for the soft body. So right here I'm just going to re-add my cube and collision plane right here. And on the cube I'm going to subdivide it twice. And let's go ahead and take a look at Self-collision. Now the Self-collision is basically going to allow us to control or prevent the soft body from intersecting with itself. How it does this is it's going to surround every vertex with a ball. And this ball size is going to be surrounding the vertices. It's going to be basically an invisible elastic virtual ball, and the vertices can't penetrate the balls of other vertices. Now this only works if edges is enabled. You can see that here. If I enable Self-collision and disable edges, you can see that. Let's disable goal as well. You can see that it doesn't work. So edges has to be enabled for Self-collision to take effect. If it's not, self-collision won't work. So you have to have edges enabled. So right here you can see we have different calculation methods. Don't worry. It's all the same settings on all of them. So with it set to average the size is going to be determined by the average length of the edges that are attached to the vertices. And again this will be scaled by the ball size right here. So right here you can see it's going to take the average length right here. And then it's going to scale it based on this size. So if I play this you can see we have this right here with it's set to 0.49. If I increase this you can see that we have this right here. You can see it inflates because again it's making it so that these vertices which have these balls are not going to intersect or self collide with each other. So you can see what we get right there. If I bring it to a negative number, you could see that it basically implodes on itself. If I bring it to a very high number like ten, you can see we get this right here. So again with it set to average, it's going to average the length of all the edges and then determine it also based on the ball size. So right here for example if I just grab these vertices and hit g and y and bring these out, it will now take the average of these edges and these ones. And let me scale up the plane a little bit. And now you can see that with it set to average. We have this right here where again it's going to take the average of the length of these edges and these ones and then scale it by the ball size. Then we have manual right here where manual is going to set the exact size of these virtual collision balls around each vertex. So you can see here if I change this it's going to set the exact size and it's not going to average it with the length of the edges. Then right here we have minimal. So with it set to minimal, it's going to use the smallest edge length to determine the ball size. And then obviously scale it by the ball size here. So here obviously we can see that the smallest edge lengths are these ones right here as these ones are much larger. So if I play this you can see it's taking these edge lengths for the ball size and then scaling it by this. Whereas if I change it to maximal right here with maximal it's going to use the largest edge length to determine the ball size. So here it's going to use these edge lengths to determine the ball size. And so you can see the difference with maximal and minimal right here. Very cool. And of course like I said the ball size will basically scale or multiply the edge length that is taken from whatever calculation type we use. All right then we have average minimum and maximum. Now this is going to average the smallest and largest edge lengths to set the ball size. So it's going to average the largest ones and the smallest ones. So you can see here what we get right there. So you can see with average maximal minimal average and manual. So again manual you set the ball size average. It will average all the edges minimal. It will take the smallest edges maximal it will take the largest edges. And average minimum maximum it will average the smallest and largest edge lengths. All right. Very cool. Let's go ahead and set this back to average then. Right here we have ball size. Obviously this is going to define the radius of these virtual balls. So if another vertex let's say that this vertex has a certain ball size. If this vertex enters the radius of the ball of this vertex it will be repelled to prevent self collisions or intersections. Then we have stiffness right here. The stiffness is going to control how quickly the vertices are going to respond to the nearby collisions. So the higher we have this it's going to create a higher repulsion force and it's going to be stronger and more immediate. So here you can see at one we get this. If I increase this to let's say 59 you can see right here we get this. So again this is how quickly it's going to respond to the nearby collisions. You can see if I have it at 0 or 0.001. We don't have much. If I set this to one you can see it responds that fast. If I put it to 11 you can see it responds a lot faster. So again this is the stiffness. So basically a high stiffness means that the vertex is going to react immediately to another vertex entering its space. Whereas if the stiffness is lower it won't react immediately, but it will be a little slower. Then we have the dampening right here. The dampening is going to be how the vertex reacts to the self-collision. So you can see here, if I put this to a lower value, you can see right here, it explodes immediately and then settles in that state. Whereas if I put it to a high value like 0.9, you can see it's a much more gradual effect and then it dampens out and just rests in this initial state, as you can see right here. So this is basically going to control how smoothly the vertices move away from each other when they collide. You can see a higher value. They move more slowly and more smoothly away from each other, whereas a lower value, they will move more abruptly away from each other. All right. So that is the self-collision. ### Dynamic Paint Settings

All right. In this section we're going to go ahead and take a look at dynamic paint which is super awesome. Dynamic paint basically allows for us to add an object that is a canvas and one that is a brush. And then we're able to create things such as footsteps in the snow or raindrops that make the ground wet, or paint being painted on a wall. Or for example, if we need paint being scratched off a wall, etc.. So a dynamic paint is very versatile and allows for us to do a lot of things again, allows for us to dynamically paint on our objects. So here let's go ahead. Let's delete the cube.
