### Domain Settings

All right. Let's go ahead and take a look at the settings for the fire and smoke simulation. So once again we're going to the domain which is this bounding box. And right here once again we have the type which is set to domain. And then down here we have the settings. So we're going to take a look at the settings first right here we have domain type. We have either gas which is for smoke and fire or liquid which is obviously for liquid. So let's leave it to gas. We'll take a look at liquid or water in another section then right here we have the resolution divisions. Right here. The resolution divisions is going to be the amount of grid cells or voxels. Again we took a look at voxels before that are within the domain. So this is basically going to be the amount of pixels or resolution in our fire or simulation. So here the lower the resolution divisions is the lower resolution the fire or simulation will be. And the higher the higher resolution, obviously the more this is increased, the more intensive it's going to be on your computer. So again this is going to be the resolution of the voxels. Now again these voxels are basically three dimensional pixels. So in 2D you have pixels that represent the resolution of an image. In 3D we have voxels which are three dimensional pixels which are going to represent the resolution of the simulation. So each voxel or 3D pixel is going to store information about the fluid simulation such as density and velocity and more. And then the resolution of our simulation is going to have to do with the number of voxels. Again, the higher voxels or resolution subdivisions, the more resolution and the better it will look. So here again you don't have to do this. I'm just going to show you a visual representation of the voxels. Again, don't have to do this. But here let me go into wireframe. Let me add this cube here and I'm going to scale it down like so. And let me add an array modifier and increase this like so. And then here I'm going to go ahead and duplicate this. ### Border Collisions & Adaptive Domain

All right. The next two settings that are under the settings tab right here are border collisions and adaptive domain. Now the border collisions right here is basically going to dictate which sides or which borders of our domain are going to allow for fluid or fire or smoke. Again when I say fluid that references fluid simulation, fire simulation, smoke simulation, etc.. So the border collisions is going to dictate whether the fluid will pass through or basically disappear when it hits a border, or whether it will be deflected back and bounce back off of those borders or sides. So you can see right here with border collision, we could enable the border collision for the front, back, right, left, top and bottom of the domain with nothing enabled. You can see that once any of the smoke or fire hits a certain side of the domain, you can see it just disappears. But if I enable all of these right here by left clicking and dragging down like so, you can see that here. Once the smoke hits the border, it will basically bounce back off that border and then fill the domain. It is no longer passing through the borders or just disappearing when it hits the border, but rather the border is deflecting the smoke back and then it's being contained in here. If I enable just the top. So again, left clicking and dragging to deselect a lot at a time. If I select just the top, you can see that the top is going to deflect it, but then it's going to be able to go out of the sides because we don't have any of the sides enabled. If I enable right and left, you can see that here it will only be able to go out of the front and back, but not the right and left side if I enable the back and front as well. Now it could only go out the bottom because that's the only one that's not enabled, as you can see right there. If I disable right and left, you can see we have this right here, etc.. So again with these disabled the smoke will just disappear or pass through. And with these enabled the smoke will be deflected and bounce back. And it will basically act as an actual container. The cache is basically used for baking or storing the results of the simulation so that it doesn't have to recalculate it every single time. So basically it stores all of the settings and our simulation so that we don't have to again calculate it every single time we run it. So here you can see we have a frame start and end for the cache. So depending on the length of your animation, you're going to want to set the start and end frame correctly. Then right here you can see under type we have three different types. So we have replay right here. So here with it set to replay the cache is going to be baked while it's playing in the viewport. So this is what it's set to by default. Then right here we have modular with it's set to modular. Here the cache will be baked step by step. Now the bake operations are going to be spread throughout the various different simulations and objects. For example once again with modular under guides, you could see that here. If we change it to effector, we could bake the guides here. And we have different baking panels for example right here bake data as you can see. So you can see right here we have bake all and this will bake the guides. It will bake the simulation up here everything. So this will bake all the steps at once. VDB stands for voxel data base. So this file format is going to be an efficient file format. And it's basically going to store volumetric data such as here smoke or fire or other fluid simulations such as water. And here it's going to represent the volumetric data in a way where it's only going to store cells or voxels. Again, VDB. So it's only going to store cells or voxels that have information about the simulation or relevant information. So this is going to help to reduce the memory usage. So basically once again this format is going to store the information that is in the voxels. Again Openvdb standing for voxel database. So again we took a look at the voxels which is the 3D pixel grid for the simulation. And this is storing that information of the voxels. Now what's really cool about this. Let's go ahead and click on Bake All. So right here if I click on bake all right there it's going to go ahead and bake it. And there we go. So now we've baked it. So here obviously we could play this and it's baked. You could also see that when you bake it all of the settings are locked in because it's basically cached it or baked it. And to change the settings you need to click on Free All. But what's really cool with Openvdb is you can see here in our folder under the data. These are dot vdb files, as you can see right there. Now what's really awesome with this is if I go ahead and just move this to the side. So let me just move that to the side. Pretty freaking cool. So let me go ahead and delete that and then lastly here on the settings, you can see that on Openvdb we have an advanced tab right here. Let me click on Free All. And right here we just have the compression and precision volume right here. So the compression volume right here is basically going to determine how it compresses the VDB files. Now first right here we have it set to block by default with block. This is a multithreaded compression that is going to be slightly faster than zip. And this is good for a balance of speed and compression. And then right here we have zip. Now the zip compression is going to compress it with zip compression. And this is going to provide good compression rates. But it can also be slower especially if we have larger data. And then lastly we have none. We're right here. It's not going to be compressed meaning that the file sizes will be really large. But they will be faster with writing and reading speeds. Again, right here we have none. Again, no compression, bigger files, but it will be faster with writing and reading. Block is like an intermediate between none and zip, where it gives good speed and good compression and zip compression right here will write it with zip compression, and this is slightly slower than block. So by default it's set to blast. You'll probably just leave it to that by default. Then right here we have the precision volume. By default it's set to half. Half is going to mean the volumetric data, such as the grids or particles will be written with half the precision or 16 bit. Then we have full write here with it set to full means the volumetric data. Again the grids or particles will be written with full precision or 32 bits of information. So again full will be larger files of 32 bit information. And this will be half or 16 bit information. And that is pretty much all for the cash. Again you can see that we don't have those options on uni cash. As you can see right there. That is only for openvdb. So with that I'll see you in the next one. Ciao for now. Oliver.

## Liquid Simulations

### Liquid Overview

All right. It is time for the fluid section of the course. Now, one thing to note, fluid is the one thing in blender that I don't like too much. It can be a little bit glitchy and a little bit buggy, and sometimes it doesn't work as expected. I love everything about blender, but the fluid simulation is the one thing that I don't like that much. Now, if you really want to get into fluid simulation in blender, there is an add on called Flip Fluids, which I recommend getting if you're going to dive deep into fluid simulations. But if you're not diving deep into it, you could just use the built in fluid simulation that we have here that we're going to take a look at. So here first things first. Let's see how this works. Now we're not going to have to take a look at that much settings because a lot of the settings are the same as the fire and smoke simulation which is awesome. Now here once again we could add this manually. So for example we could have a domain for example this cube. Let's go into edit mode scale it up. ### Liquid Diffusion

Water has a lower viscosity than something like honey, so the higher the viscosity it means it's going to be thicker liquid, like honey or syrup. And if we have lower viscosity, it's going to represent more fluid, like liquids, like water. So right here you can see if I now play this, it looks the same. So if I disable it and play it and if I enable it and play it, you can see it looks the same. And that's because right here the viscosity settings or the base and exponent are for water. So right here we have a base and exponent. These work together. They work in conjunction with each other. Now the base right here is going to be the main number. And the exponent right here is going to be the power of ten applied to the base. Now this exponent is a negative number. So even if we have six this is a negative six. So for example right here let me go ahead and get the annotation tool right here. If we have a base of one it's going to be one times our exponent. So it's going to be one times ten. Again this is the power of ten with whatever number we have here. So in this case it's going to be one times ten to the negative sixth power. So it's one times ten to the negative six. If we set this for example to two or something it's going to be one times ten to the power of negative two. And you're probably thinking great how do I use this practically well over here. If we go to Google and here on Google just type in blender fluid diffusion and here on the blender manual. We have this page right here. Now normally in the real world, the viscosity of something is measured in CP or Centipoise units, as you can see right here. Again, you could feel free to read this to get a better understanding of it. But again viscosity is measured in CP or Centipoise units. So right here you can see we have the viscosity for water oil honey chocolate syrup ketchup and melting glass. And right here these are the values right here in centipoise units or in the real world. But in blender it calculates it differently. So these right here are the numbers converted from the centipoise units or the real world units to the blender units. So right here for example if I go ahead and take a look at this chart, you can see that water for the first number or the base right here. It's going to be 1.002. So if I type in 1.002 right here, we have that. And then we can see that the exponent is -6 or 6. Again this is just a negative value by default. So if I put six it's going to be water. So now we have the viscosity of water again the thickness of water or how water behaves. If we want oil you can see right here it's five. So I need to put the base to five. And the exponent is negative five. So I need to put this to five. And now you can see that here we have the viscosity of oil or how oil would act. If we want honey we need to put two for the base and the exponent of three. So if I put two and three you can see that here. Now we have honey. As you can see right there, if I want chocolate syrup I need three to the power of 3 or -3. So here if I play this you can see here I have chocolate syrup. And then ketchup is going to be one and one right there, or negative one. And you can see that right here I have chocolate syrup and you can see what that looks like. And then melting glass is going to be one to the power of zero. So I need to put that to zero. And you can see that here. We now have melting glass. Pretty cool. So that is the different viscosity or base and exponent settings. Again you can refer this page to see which settings you need for different types of fluids. All right there we go. Let me hit S shift Z to scale this up like so. Now the surface tension is going to have to do with the force that makes the liquid behave like a stretched elastic sheet. So again, the surface tension is going to be when the molecules at the surface of the liquid are more attracted to each other than the air. So it's going to cause them to stick together tightly. This is what causes small objects or insects that can sit on the water without sinking, and what forms water droplets. So here the surface tension is going to determine how much the liquid particles cling together. So it's going to affect the liquid's ability to form shapes like droplets or other shapes with the water, or to spread out smoothly. Now, the issue with this here is that in the current version of blender, this option does not work. You can see at zero we got that, and at 100 we have this right here and it's not working.
